prompt:
# Lesson Reconciliation Prompt

## Mission

Support the two internal Lesson Reconciliation tasks for exactly one Lesson:

- `lesson_candidate_clustering`: group candidate IDs only.
- `lesson_cluster_evaluation`: evaluate one validated cluster or a small batch
  of validated clusters into clean lesson-local teachable concepts.
- `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`: repair a deterministic Phase 4b
  quality failure for targeted candidates only.

The input candidates come from Self-study Extraction and Metadata-only
Extraction. There is no top-down lesson extraction in this pipeline branch.

## Quick Start

First inspect `task`.

If `task` is `lesson_candidate_clustering`, return clusters only. Every
`input_candidate_ids` item must appear exactly once across cluster `candidate_ids`.
Do not create accepted concepts, pruning decisions, evidence, or provenance.

If `task` is `lesson_cluster_evaluation`, read the provided `clusters`,
`candidates`, and `input_candidate_ids`. Create the smallest clean set of
lesson-local concepts for those clusters only. Return accepted concepts plus one
`candidate_assignments` row for every input ID in the batch.

If `task` is `lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, read the quality audit,
current reconciled candidates, and target candidates. Decide whether each target
candidate should be represented by a new accepted concept, merged into an
existing accepted concept, or pruned. Do not return `review`.

## Concept Standard

A lesson-local concept is one teachable idea small enough for the Companion to
check with one to three focused questions. It is not a source title, activity,
workbook label, technology name, vague topic, name-drop, incidental mention, or
tiny fragment that belongs inside a stronger concept.

Source-backed does not automatically mean lesson-worthy. A candidate can be
grounded in a source and still be incidental, off-lesson, too broad,
administrative, setup-oriented, or better represented inside another concept.
Accept only candidates that fit the Lesson's title, description, related labels,
and candidate evidence as teachable content for this Lesson.

## Clustering Workflow

1. Group duplicates and near-duplicates that likely describe the same teachable
   idea in this Lesson.
2. Keep distinct prerequisite, implementation, evaluation, or application ideas
   in separate clusters.
3. Prefer small coherent clusters over broad topic buckets.
4. Put operational setup, installation, licensing, career, administrative, and
   generic programming candidates in their own clusters unless the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes them central content.
5. Do not prune during clustering unless an input is clearly unrelated to the
   Lesson; if uncertain, put it in its own cluster for evaluation.
6. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across all clusters. Never
   emit empty clusters or invented candidate IDs.

## Evaluation Workflow

1. Treat Source Body candidates as the strongest evidence.
2. Merge duplicates and near-duplicates across Self-studies when they teach the
   same idea inside the provided cluster batch.
3. Split compound or messy candidates into cleaner accepted concepts when one
   input candidate supports multiple teachable ideas.
4. Accept Metadata-only candidates only when Workbook Metadata fills a real
   lesson gap not already covered by Source Body candidates.
5. Prefer lesson coherence over source-by-source preservation, but never drop a
   source-backed candidate silently.
6. Preserve useful granularity. Do not merge distinct definitions, pipeline
   steps, limitations, implementation methods, evaluation methods, or
   applications merely because they share a broad topic.
7. Reject off-lesson or low-transfer material even when it is source-backed:
   setup commands, environment configuration, licensing/legal administration,
   certification/career advice, repository mechanics, dataset download
   utilities, and routine file I/O should be accepted only when the Lesson
   metadata clearly makes that material central teachable content.
8. Use `used_in` when a candidate directly supports one or more accepted
   concepts.
9. Use `merged_into` when a candidate should not stand alone but is represented
   by one accepted concept.
10. Use `pruned` only when the candidate should not influence the lesson concept
   set at all. Use only a reason from `controlled_pruning_reasons`.
11. Do not prune a distinct teachable idea as a duplicate unless an accepted
   concept in this same response actually represents it. Never justify pruning
   by saying another cluster, later batch, or future step will handle the idea.
12. Avoid `review`. Phase 4 has no human review escape hatch. If the lesson
   metadata, candidate description, source roles, and coverage criteria are
   sufficient, decide accepted, merged, or pruned.
13. Use `review` only when the input is structurally impossible to interpret.
   Phase 4b will treat any review output as unresolved work requiring repair.

## Quality Repair Workflow

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`:

1. Evaluate only `target_candidate_ids`; do not rewrite the whole Lesson.
2. Use `current_reconciled_candidates` to decide whether a target candidate is
   already represented.
3. Create `new_accepted_concepts` only for target candidates that represent
   lesson-worthy teachable ideas not already covered.
4. Use `existing_concept_candidate_additions` when a target candidate is
   represented by an existing reconciled concept.
5. Use `pruned` only when the target candidate should not influence the Lesson.
6. Never return `review`. A hard choice must still become accepted, merged, or
   pruned with a clear explanation.
7. Do not use a duplicate or near-duplicate reason unless the target candidate
   is represented by an existing or new accepted concept in this response.
8. If the audit flags `over_pruned`, re-check pruned target candidates for
   lesson-local definitions, methods, steps, limitations, evaluations, or
   applications that were lost by an overly broad pruning decision.
9. If the audit flags `over_merged`, split target candidates out of broad
   accepted concepts when they contain distinct lesson-local ideas.
10. If the audit flags `fragmented_duplicates`, merge duplicate accepted
   concepts by assigning target candidates to the best existing concept.
11. If the audit flags `metadata_overreach`, accept metadata-only targets only
   when they fill a lesson gap not already covered by source-body evidence.
12. If the audit flags `off_lesson_accepted`, prune setup, repository,
   administration, download, career, or generic tooling material unless the
   Lesson metadata clearly makes it central teachable content.
13. If the audit flags `over_accepted`, re-check whether target candidates
   should be merged into stronger accepted concepts or pruned for low teaching
   value.

## Clustering Output Contract

For `task: lesson_candidate_clustering`, return one valid JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short cluster label",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may describe the same teachable idea.",
      "candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Evaluation Output Contract

For `task: lesson_cluster_evaluation`, return one valid JSON object only. Cover
all candidates in the provided cluster batch:

```json
{
  "accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "lr001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these candidates form one lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["lr001"]
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "represented-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "lr001",
      "explanation": "Why it is represented by lr001 instead of standing alone."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "incidental",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "discarded-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "unrelated",
      "explanation": "Why this candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Quality Repair Output Contract

For `task: lesson_reconciliation_quality_repair`, return one valid JSON object
only:

```json
{
  "new_accepted_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "repair001",
      "label": "Specific lesson-local teachable idea",
      "description": "What the student needs to understand in this Lesson.",
      "coverage_criteria": ["Observable check in one to three focused questions."],
      "source_candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "merge_rationale": "Why these target candidates form a lesson-local concept."
    }
  ],
  "existing_concept_candidate_additions": [
    {
      "reconciled_candidate_id": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "candidate_ids": ["target-compact-candidate-id"],
      "explanation": "Why the target candidate is already represented."
    }
  ],
  "candidate_assignments": [
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "used_in",
      "accepted_ids": ["repair001"],
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is accepted."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "merged_into",
      "merged_into": "existing-final-reconciled-candidate-id",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate is represented by an existing concept."
    },
    {
      "candidate_id": "target-compact-candidate-id",
      "status": "pruned",
      "reason": "low_teaching_value",
      "explanation": "Why this target candidate should not influence the lesson set."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-check

- For clustering, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once across
  all cluster `candidate_ids`.
- For evaluation, every `input_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`.
- Every `used_in` or `merged_into` assignment references accepted concept IDs
  that also list that candidate in `source_candidate_ids`.
- A candidate may support multiple accepted concepts with `used_in`.
- A `pruned` or `review` candidate must not appear in any accepted concept's
  `source_candidate_ids`.
- Every pruned near-duplicate must be represented by an accepted concept in this
  response, or it should not be pruned as a duplicate.
- For quality repair, every `target_candidate_ids` item appears exactly once in
  `candidate_assignments`, and no assignment has `status: review`.
- If several accepted concepts are mainly setup, environment, licensing,
  administration, career guidance, or generic programming basics, re-check the
  Lesson metadata before accepting them.
- Before returning, ask whether the accepted concept set would let the Companion
  tutor the Lesson described by the metadata without major off-topic detours or
  missing central teachable distinctions.
- Do not emit dependencies, lesson segments, final Concept IDs, bridge concepts,
  subject-level merge decisions, or runtime graph fields.

lesson.description: O objetivo deste encontro é aplicar o conceito de rede neurais apresentados nos encontros anteriores em conjunto com o Word2Vec para construção de aplicações.

repair_plan.explanation: Review is not allowed as a final Phase 4 state.

target_candidates.label: Nearest Neighbor Search in Vector Space
target_candidates.description: Given a vector space and a query vector, the closest neighbors can be found by computing distances to all items and selecting the smallest ones.
coverage_criteria: Describe the process of scanning all vectors to find the closest one.
Explain why naive nearest neighbor search is inefficient for large spaces.
Identify that the closest() function in the source implements this by sorting by distance.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates a closest() function that finds the ten closest color names to a given RGB value, and mentions scalability issues and alternatives like kdtree or Annoy.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept isolates the basic algorithm for nearest neighbor, a core operation in vector-based retrieval, without diving into optimized indexing structures.

target_candidates.label: Finding similar words with model.similar_by_word()
target_candidates.description: The method similar_by_word() on a trained Word2Vec model returns the most semantically similar words to a given word and their similarity scores.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to retrieve the top-5 similar words for 'car' using similar_by_word and interpret the results.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 7 on pages 200-201 uses similar_by_word to find words similar to 'car' and 'house', showing the cosine similarity scores.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Covers one method of the model; can be checked with a short coding exercise.

anchors: Example 7 – Palavras similares a car e house, page 201

target_candidates.label: Vector Arithmetic Operations
target_candidates.description: Vectors can be added, subtracted, and averaged component-wise, enabling combination and comparison of concepts represented as vectors.
coverage_criteria: Add two vectors by summing corresponding components.
Subtract one vector from another to find the difference.
Compute the mean of a list of vectors.
Explain how the mean vector represents the 'center' of a set of vectors.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides functions addv, subtractv, meanv in Python code within the color vectors section and uses them for color arithmetic, demonstrating how vector operations correspond to combining colors.
rationale.granularity_rationale: The concept covers basic vector algebra operations that are essential for later analogies and sentence averaging, and is testable with simple component-wise calculations.

target_candidates.label: Analogies through Vector Differences
target_candidates.description: Analogies can be solved by subtracting the vector of one word from another and adding the difference to a third word's vector, e.g., 'pink is to red as X is to blue'.
coverage_criteria: Given vectors for 'pink', 'red', and 'blue', compute the vector for X that satisfies 'pink - red = X - blue'.
Explain that the difference vector captures the relationship between two words.
Provide an example of an analogy derived from a vector space.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly demonstrates analogies with color vectors (pink:red::?:blue) and with animal vectors (tarantula:hamster::chicken:kitten), showing that vector differences can model relational similarity.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific application of vector arithmetic that is central to word vector 'magic'; it is a single skill that can be tested with a small computation.

anchors: Animal similarity and simple linear algebra

target_candidates.label: Word Vectors from Co-occurrence Counts
target_candidates.description: Word vectors can be constructed by counting how often each word appears in each possible context (e.g., neighboring words), forming a high-dimensional vector per word.
coverage_criteria: Explain how a co-occurrence matrix is built from a text corpus.
Given a small corpus, construct a simple co-occurrence matrix.
Identify that the resulting vector for a word reflects its distributional context.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source walks through creating a spreadsheet from a Dickens sentence, counting word contexts, and explaining that the counts form word vectors, with 'best' and 'worst' having identical vectors because they appear in the same context.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept introduces the concrete method of turning text into vectors, a key step in understanding word embeddings; it is small enough to test with a simple example.

target_candidates.label: Dimensionality Reduction for Word Vectors
target_candidates.description: High-dimensional word vectors from co-occurrence counts often contain redundant information; dimensionality reduction techniques (like SVD) can compress them into a smaller number of meaningful dimensions.
coverage_criteria: Explain why raw co-occurrence vectors can be too high-dimensional.
Name dimensionality reduction as a solution.
State that typical word vectors have 100-300 dimensions after reduction.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source discusses that many dimensions are superfluous and can be eliminated or combined via dimensionality reduction, mentioning that count-based vectors often use 100-300 dimensions.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This concept bridges the gap between raw counts and practical word embeddings; it is a single technique that can be tested by asking why reduction is needed and what dimensions are typical.

target_candidates.label: Pre-trained GloVe Word Vectors
target_candidates.description: GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation) is a set of pre-trained 300-dimensional word vectors available in spaCy, providing a ready-to-use semantic space for English.
coverage_criteria: State that GloVe vectors are 300-dimensional and pre-trained.
Identify that GloVe vectors are included in spaCy's 'en' model.
Explain that using pre-trained vectors saves the effort of training on a corpus.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces GloVe as a downloadable database of pre-trained vectors from Stanford, included with spaCy, and states they will be used for the rest of the tutorial.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a practical resource concept, informing students that they can leverage existing vectors; it's small and testable with factual recall.

target_candidates.label: Using pre-trained word embeddings with gensim.downloader
target_candidates.description: The gensim.downloader module allows loading publicly available pre-trained models like word2vec-google-news-300, which provides high-quality embeddings for downstream tasks.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to load a pre-trained model using gensim.downloader.load() and cite an example such as 'word2vec-google-news-300'.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 6 on page 200 demonstrates loading a pre-trained model, and the text explains the benefits of using large pre-trained embeddings.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Single function with a clear purpose; testable with a code snippet and recognition of common models.

anchors: Example 6 – Carregando um modelo pré-treinado, page 200

target_candidates.label: Sentence Similarity via Averaged Word Vectors
target_candidates.description: A sentence vector can be obtained by averaging the word vectors of its constituent words, and this can be used to find semantically similar sentences in a corpus.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to compute a sentence vector from word vectors.
Compute the average of multiple word vectors (component-wise).
Describe that cosine similarity between sentence vectors can measure sentence similarity.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source defines a sentvec() function that averages word vectors of a sentence, then uses it with spacy_closest_sent() to find sentences in Dracula similar to a query, yielding plausible results.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a specific technique for extending word vectors to longer texts, small enough to test by having students compute a mean and interpret similarity.

target_candidates.label: Word Vector Arithmetic with Pre-trained Embeddings
target_candidates.description: Arithmetic on GloVe word vectors can reveal meaningful semantic relationships, e.g., 'water' + 'frozen' yields 'ice', and 'wine' - 'alcohol' yields words like 'dinner'.
coverage_criteria: Perform vector addition or subtraction with GloVe vectors (hypothetically) and interpret results.
Explain that such arithmetic reflects learned semantic relationships from training data.
Given example arithmetic, predict plausible results based on semantic intuition.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates several examples: 'wine' - 'alcohol' returns food-related words, 'water' + 'frozen' returns 'ice', 'blue' - 'sky' + 'grass' returns 'green', showing that pre-trained vectors encode relationships.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a practical skill demonstrating the 'magic' of word vectors, combining vector arithmetic and pre-trained embeddings in a testable way.

anchors: Fun with spaCy, Dracula, and vector arithmetic

target_candidates.label: Gensim library for topic modeling and NLP
target_candidates.description: Gensim is an open-source Python library originally developed for topic modeling, providing models and utilities for unsupervised text analysis including Word2Vec and preprocessing.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that Gensim is a Python library for NLP, mention its origin in topic modeling, and name at least two of its functionalities (e.g., Word2Vec, preprocessing, dictionary creation).

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The chapter introduces Gensim as a tool for topic modeling and highlights its use in NLP, starting from page 189.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Concept covers the library's identity and purpose; assessable in a few questions about its role and capabilities.

target_candidates.label: Text preprocessing with gensim.utils.simple_preprocess()
target_candidates.description: The function simple_preprocess() tokenizes a document, optionally removing accents and filtering tokens by minimum and maximum length.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to call simple_preprocess() on a string, specifying parameters deacc, min_len, max_len, and explain what each does.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 1 on pages 192-193 demonstrates using simple_preprocess with deacc and min_len, and the surrounding text explains the parameters.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Single function with a clear interface; can be checked with a coding exercise and explanation of parameters.

anchors: Example 1 – Definição de um corpus e pré-processamento, page 193

target_candidates.label: Tokenization with gensim.utils.tokenize()
target_candidates.description: The gensim.utils.tokenize() function performs low-level tokenization, internally called by simple_preprocess(), and can be used directly for tokenizing words.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that tokenize() splits text into tokens and is less feature-rich than simple_preprocess, and can write a call to tokenize().

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Page 194 mentions tokenize() as an alternative for word tokenization, stating it is called internally by simple_preprocess.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Narrow concept focusing on one utility function; can be assessed with a simple usage question.

target_candidates.label: Building a vocabulary with gensim.corpora.Dictionary()
target_candidates.description: gensim.corpora.Dictionary creates a mapping between tokens and integer IDs from preprocessed documents, acting as the model's vocabulary.
coverage_criteria: Given a list of tokenized documents, student can instantiate a Dictionary and explain its purpose in encoding words.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 2 on pages 194-195 uses corpDict to build a vocabulary from preprocessed documents, and the text describes its necessity before model creation.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Concept covers a single class and its main role; easily testable with a code snippet and brief explanation.

anchors: Example 2 – Vocabulário criado a partir dos documentos tokenizados e tratados, page 194

target_candidates.label: Training a Word2Vec model with gensim.models.Word2Vec()
target_candidates.description: The Word2Vec class in Gensim trains word embeddings on a preprocessed corpus using continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) or skip-gram with options for hierarchical softmax or negative sampling.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to instantiate Word2Vec with a list of tokenized sentences, specify min_count and size, and explain that the model learns vector representations.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 3 on page 196 trains a Word2Vec model and the surrounding text explains the usage and parameters.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Covers the central API for Word2Vec training; can be assessed with a coding task and a question on basic parameters.

anchors: Example 3 – Treinamento de um modelo de word2vec, page 196

target_candidates.label: Word2Vec training parameters
target_candidates.description: Key parameters for gensim.models.Word2Vec() include min_count, size, sg (0: skip-gram, 1: CBOW), window, hs (hierarchical softmax), negative (negative sampling), alpha (learning rate), seed, and corpus_file.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least four training parameters and explain how they affect the training process.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Pages 196-198 detail many parameters for Word2Vec, explaining each in the context of training.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Combines multiple related parameters into a single concept about model configuration; can be tested with a matching or short-answer question.

target_candidates.label: Saving and loading Word2Vec models
target_candidates.description: Gensim Word2Vec models can be saved to disk using save() and reloaded later with load(), facilitating reuse of trained embeddings.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to save a trained model to a file and load it back using gensim's save and load methods.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 4 (page 198-199) saves a model and Example 5 (page 199) loads it, explicitly showing the workflow.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Narrow concept around two functions; easily checked with code completion.

anchors: Example 4 – Armazenando um modelo de word2vec, page 198

target_candidates.label: Dense versus sparse vector representations
target_candidates.description: Documents can be represented as vectors; dense vectors have all dimensions known and directly related, while sparse vectors have many unknown dimensions treated as zero.
coverage_criteria: Student can define dense and sparse vectors and give an example of when each would be used in text representation.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Page 195 explicitly contrasts dense and sparse vectors, defining each and stating that unknown dimensions in sparse vectors are zero.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Concept is a foundational distinction in vector representations; assessable with a definition and simple scenario.

target_candidates.label: Brown Corpus as a standard NLP dataset
target_candidates.description: The Brown Corpus is a collection of 500 English texts from 1961 containing over 1 million words, commonly used for NLP model training and evaluation.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the Brown Corpus (size, date, types of texts) and explain why it is a valuable resource for NLP.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: Example 4 uses the Brown Corpus from NLTK, and page 199 describes its origin and size, noting its frequent use in NLP.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Concept introduces a well-known dataset; can be assessed with a few factual questions.

target_candidates.label: Neural networks can learn word embeddings from a fake problem
target_candidates.description: Instead of hand-crafting features, word embeddings are learned as a side effect of training a neural network on an auxiliary task, like predicting a missing word.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain that the primary goal is to obtain word vectors, and the network is trained on a surrogate task such as filling in a blank.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video explains taking a 'fake problem' (filling missing word) to learn embeddings as a side effect.
rationale.granularity_rationale: This is a key conceptual leap distinguishing manual feature engineering from learned embeddings.

anchors: [04:00] Learning Word Embeddings with Neural Networks

target_candidates.label: Word2Vec is a self-supervised learning approach
target_candidates.description: The training data (input-output pairs) is generated from the raw text itself without external labels, making it self-supervised.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain that Word2Vec does not require manually labeled data; the labels come from the text itself through the windowing process.

rationale.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions 'this problem is called self-supervised because all you had was this paragraph you did not have like X and Y' and you generate training samples.
rationale.granularity_rationale: Self-supervision is an important concept in machine learning, and Word2Vec is a classic example.

anchors: [07:41] Generating Training Samples for Word Embeddings

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Distributional Hypothesis of Meaning
current_reconciled_candidates.description: The distributional hypothesis states that words with similar meanings occur in similar contexts. This concept covers the idea that a word's meaning can be inferred from the company it keeps, demonstrated through contextual inference examples.
coverage_criteria: State the distributional hypothesis.
Given example sentences, identify words that are likely semantically related based on shared contexts.
Explain why antonyms like 'hot' and 'cold' can be considered similar under this hypothesis.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates describe the same fundamental idea that meaning arises from context; c61_pro_thinking_005 provides the formal statement, while c63_pro_thinking_004 offers practical demonstration with sentence completion.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Word Vectors as Numerical Representations
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Words can be encoded as vectors of numbers, where each dimension represents a semantic or descriptive feature such as authority, richness, or gender. This concept forms the basis for representing text data in a continuous vector space.
coverage_criteria: Explain that a word vector is a numerical encoding of a word's features.
Provide examples of possible features for a given word (e.g., 'king' could have high authority, male, royalty).
Distinguish between hand-crafted features and automatically learned features.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as the foundational building block for understanding how words are represented before discussing learning algorithms.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Vector Arithmetic for Semantic Analogies
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Word vectors learned by Word2Vec support vector arithmetic that reflects semantic relationships, enabling analogy solving (e.g., 'king' - 'man' + 'woman' ≈ 'queen').
coverage_criteria: Given a word vector equation, predict the expected result word for a simple analogy.
Explain that vector difference can capture the relationship between two words.
Perform vector addition or subtraction to solve an analogy task.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: c63_pro_thinking_001 introduces the concept of arithmetic with word vectors, and c63_pro_thinking_011 provides specific concrete examples; together they cover the skill of using vector arithmetic to express analogies.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Semantic and Syntactic Relationships in Word2Vec Embeddings
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Word2Vec embeddings capture a variety of linguistic relationships, including verb tenses, capital-country associations, and gender pairs, by encoding them as consistent vector offsets.
coverage_criteria: Provide at least two distinct types of linguistic relationships that word vectors can capture (e.g., tense, geography).
Explain why such relationships emerge from the training objective.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as an overview of the emergent properties of Word2Vec vectors, distinct from the mechanics of arithmetic.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Similarity Measures for Word Vectors
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Euclidean distance and cosine similarity are two metrics used to quantify the similarity between word vectors. Euclidean distance measures straight-line distance in vector space, while cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, often preferred in high-dimensional spaces.
coverage_criteria: Calculate Euclidean distance between two vectors.
Compute cosine similarity between two vectors.
Explain the differences between Euclidean distance and cosine similarity and when each might be more appropriate.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These two candidates cover complementary similarity metrics that are typically introduced together in the context of vector spaces; combining them creates a coherent concept on measuring proximity.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Training Data Generation for Word2Vec
current_reconciled_candidates.description: How training samples are created for Word2Vec: using a sliding window to form context-target pairs, representing words with one-hot encoding, and the distinction between CBOW and Skip-gram architectures.
coverage_criteria: Given a short text and window size, generate input-output pairs with context and target words.
Explain that each word is represented as a one-hot vector of vocabulary size.
Distinguish CBOW (predict target from context) from Skip-gram (predict context from target).
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates describe essential aspects of generating training data for Word2Vec: the sliding window mechanism, one-hot representation, and the high-level CBOW/Skip-gram variants. Together they form a single coherent concept about data preparation and architectural choice.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Word Embeddings as Neural Network Weights
current_reconciled_candidates.description: In Word2Vec, the word embeddings are the learned weights connecting the one-hot input to the hidden layer (or hidden to output, depending on architecture).
coverage_criteria: Indicate that after training, the embedding for a word is extracted from the weight matrix of the neural network.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate alone explains how embeddings are obtained from the training process, demystifying a key output of Word2Vec.

current_reconciled_candidates.label: Análise de Sentimentos
current_reconciled_candidates.description: Técnicas para classificar a polaridade de textos, como positivo, negativo ou neutro.
coverage_criteria: Aplicar modelos simples para classificar sentimentos em amostras de texto.
current_reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This metadata-only candidate represents the application side of the lesson, where Word2Vec can be used for sentiment analysis. It fills a gap not covered by the source body candidates.
